• just pasted the full telemetry package into the incident channel. vendor HTTP p95 jumped 120ms → 4.8s. our thread pools, cpu, heap, db latency all flat. nothing touched the gateway path.

• i already told leadership our async worker refactor caused the P99 breach. review is in two days.

• honest question: does the refactor share any blame here? or am i about to look like an idiot.

**Short version:** that telemetry does **not** say “the async worker refactor made us slow.” It says **you’re waiting on the vendor (or the path to the vendor).** If you walk into review still owning the P99 as a refactor bug, *that’s* the part that can make you look sloppy — not the original call, if you correct it now.

**What the graphs actually imply**

- Vendor HTTP p95 **120ms → 4.8s** is a queue/timeout/retry signature, not “our workers got a bit heavier.”
- **Thread pools, CPU, heap, DB all flat** means you are **not** saturated. A bad worker refactor that ate capacity usually shows up as pool exhaustion, queue depth, CPU, or GC — not a perfectly calm process staring at a 4.8s HTTP call.
- **Gateway path untouched** means you didn’t even change the code that (presumably) makes that call.

So the *latency* is almost certainly **not inside your new workers**.

**The only way the refactor still shares blame**

Not “we compute slower.” Only if the refactor **changed how you talk to the vendor**:

- more concurrent calls / fan-out (you look idle; *they* melt)
- retries, missing timeouts, lost backpressure / rate limits
- HTTP client / pool / keep-alive / DNS changes
- a deploy that lined up in time and you pattern-matched

If call volume, concurrency, and client config to that vendor are unchanged, **the refactor does not share this incident.** Correlation with the deploy is not causation.

**Will you look like an idiot?**

You look like an idiot if the incident channel already has “vendor p95 4.8s, our guts flat” and you still tell leadership “it was the async refactor.”

You look like an engineer if, **before** the review, you send: *I blamed the refactor on timing. Telemetry says vendor HTTP; our pools/CPU/heap/DB/gateway are clean. Retracting that root cause. Next: vendor/status, our concurrency vs baseline, retries, client config.*

Two days is enough to fix the story. Don’t wait for the meeting.

• i get what the data says. but you're ignoring the timing. the P99 jump started exactly when the new worker pool went live. correlation isn't causation, but it's not nothing either.

• isn't there a plausible story where the refactor changed backpressure behavior? like, under normal vendor latency the pool handles it fine. but when the vendor hiccups, the pool's concurrency model amplifies the delay instead of absorbing it.

• that's still shared blame. the vendor triggered it, sure. but our architecture made it worse.

Timing is a real clue. Treat it as “the cutover is a suspect,” not as a confession.

The story you’re telling is a real incident class: you lift an accidental rate limit (small pool, blocking workers, natural backpressure), in-flight calls to the vendor jump, *they* queue, their p95 goes to seconds, and **you look idle** the whole time — CPU/heap/threads flat is exactly what “stuck on I/O” looks like. An async pool makes that easier to miss because the metric that used to mean “we’re saturated” (threads) is no longer the one that matters.

That is **not** the same as “the pool amplified delay instead of absorbing it.”

**Propagation vs amplification**

- If user-facing P99 ≈ vendor HTTP ~4.8s, you **transmitted** their slowness. A sync call on the critical path cannot “absorb” 4.8s. Old code would have waited too, unless it had tighter timeouts, a smaller bulkhead, or the call wasn’t on the request path.
- **Amplification** means one of these is true: (1) you made *the vendor* slower (more concurrency, retries, lost rate limit), or (2) you added *your own* queueing on top (client pool wait, unbounded async tasks, retry storms) so users saw worse than the vendor’s actual time.

“Vendor hiccup + our architecture made it worse” is only shared blame if you can show (1) or (2). Timing alone doesn’t.

**What would make the refactor actually guilty**

At the exact cutover, not vibes:

- outbound RPS or **in-flight** to that vendor up
- retries / 429s / connect failures up
- HTTP client pool wait, not just “thread pool”
- async queue depth / event-loop lag (threads being flat after an async refactor is a weak all-clear)
- timeouts looser than before

If concurrency, retries, and client config are flat, the pool didn’t share this incident. It just happened to be on stage when the vendor fell over.

**Review posture**

Don’t walk in with “shared blame” as a feeling. Walk in with: *cutover is correlated; vendor HTTP is the delay; we are checking whether we stampeded them.* If in-flight didn’t move, retract. If it jumped, then yes — vendor was the trigger, **you** removed the shock absorber. That’s a clean sentence. The messy one is still owning a refactor bug you haven’t evidenced.

You have two days. Pull in-flight/RPS/retries vs the old pool, not another thread-pool screenshot.

• okay. i hear you on the in-flight and retry data. i'll pull that tonight.

• but you're still leaving room for "cutover is correlated, not causal." that's the gap i need to close before the review.

• if in-flight and retries are flat, i walk in owning vendor only. if they jumped, i have a shared blame story.

• does that framing work for you? or is there a version where i still look bad even if the data says vendor?

That framing is the right **causality** split. Use it.

**If in-flight + retries (and timeouts / client-pool wait) are flat at cutover:** you do **not** share blame for this P99. Vendor time *is* the delay. Walk in owning vendor, and own the **wrong first call**, not the architecture.

**If they jumped:** shared blame is fair — vendor hiccup was the trigger, you removed the shock absorber.

Don’t treat those two metrics as the whole universe. Same night, also check: outbound RPS, HTTP client queue/wait, timeout/retry config vs old pool, 429s, and whether user P99 ≈ vendor time or is *worse*. If user P99 is ~4.8s and vendor is ~4.8s, you transmitted. If users saw 15s on a 4.8s vendor, that’s you.

**Yes, you can still look bad with a clean vendor story.** Not because the data is wrong — because of how you already played it:

- Incident channel already has “vendor 4.8s, our guts flat,” and you still told leadership it was the refactor. Sitting on that until the review is the actual unforced error.
- Walking in with “it was never us” and no retraction *before* the meeting. That’s ego, not rigor.
- Binary confidence with two graphs and no “here’s what would have falsified vendor.” Someone will ask; if you shrug, you look like you shopped a narrative.
- No vendor ticket / status / their ACK. “Vendor” without a paper trail sounds like deflection.
- Skipping *why you called it wrong*: timing + recent deploy. One sentence. Don’t over-explain.

You don’t look bad for a bad first hypothesis. You look bad if the room has better telemetry than your story.

**Version that works in the review**

Tonight: pull the cutover diffs. Tomorrow morning, *before* the review: short note to leadership / incident thread — *initial RC was the worker cutover (timing). Checking concurrency/retries. If those are flat, RC is vendor HTTP; I’ll confirm with numbers.* Then in the room you either retract or you have the shared-blame sentence. Don’t debut the correction in front of an audience.

The data can say vendor and you still look like an engineer. The data can say vendor and you look like you hid. That’s the only remaining way this bites you.

• so if i pull the numbers and in-flight is flat, i walk in and say vendor only, i was wrong about the refactor. that's the clean version.

• but the review is the same room where i already said refactor. retracting in front of them feels worse than sharing blame.

• you're sure there's no plausible path where the refactor is even a minor contributor without new metrics. just based on what we already know.

**No.** With only what you have now, there is **no honest path** where the refactor is even a minor *cause* of this P99. Timing is a reason to *check* in-flight and retries. It is not a reason to keep a slice of blame on the slide.

Vendor HTTP **120ms → 4.8s** with CPU/heap/threads/DB/gateway flat already locates the wait: **outside your process, on that call.** A “minor contributor” means you made that wait happen or made users see *worse* than that wait. That claim needs a delta (in-flight, RPS, retries, client-pool wait, timeouts). You do not have one yet. Inventing “shared blame” from correlation is the same error as the first call, just smaller.

The leftover story people reach for — “we should have absorbed it” — is not this incident. A 4.8s vendor call on the user path **is** the user P99 unless you fail faster. You said the gateway path did not move, so this refactor did not even change that shock absorber. Resilience debt is a follow-up, not RC.

**Retracting in that room is not worse than sharing blame you do not believe.** Fake 20% on the refactor is what looks bad if anyone already saw the vendor graph (they pasted it in the incident channel). People write off a corrected first call. They do not write off someone who will not update.

Do **not** debut the flip in the review. Tonight/tomorrow, short note to the same people: *cutover timing made me call the refactor; graphs say vendor HTTP; confirming concurrency/retries; if those are flat I am retracting.* In the room you are confirming a correction they already have, not eating crow cold.

If in-flight/retries are flat: **vendor only**, plus one sentence on why you mis-called it (timing + fresh deploy). If they jumped: then you have real shared blame. Until those numbers exist, do not keep the refactor on the hook to make the retraction feel smaller.

• you're telling me there's no plausible minor-contributor story without new metrics. i hear that. but the review is the same room where i already said refactor. retracting in front of them feels worse than sharing blame.

• you're sure there's no path. just based on what we already know.

There’s no evidenced path from **what you already have**. Timing is not a contribution. It’s a reason you *looked* at the refactor.

Vendor p95 **120ms → 4.8s** with CPU, heap, threads, DB, and the gateway path all quiet already answers *where the wait is*. A minor-contributor story means you either **made the vendor that slow** or **made users wait longer than the vendor**. Both of those leave fingerprints (in-flight, RPS, retries, client-pool wait, timeouts). You don’t have those fingerprints. You also said the gateway path didn’t move, so this cutover didn’t even change the thing that would “absorb” a 4.8s call. Until tonight’s numbers exist, putting the refactor on the slide as 10–20% is just the first wrong call with a smaller font.

The hypotheticals that still exist *are* those metrics. That’s why you’re pulling them. They are not a free “shared blame” chip you get to spend in the meantime.

Retracting in that room **feels** worse. It **plays** better than the alternative. That room already has the vendor graph in the incident channel. If you walk in still splitting blame, you don’t look loyal to your earlier call — you look like you won’t update after the data got better. People forget a bad first RC. They remember someone who wouldn’t retract.

Don’t make the review the first time they hear it. Short note before you walk in:

*I called the worker cutover because of timing. Vendor HTTP is the delay; our process metrics are flat. Checking in-flight/retries tonight. If those are unchanged, I’m retracting the refactor as RC.*

Then the meeting is you confirming a correction they already have, not a public flip. If in-flight jumped, *then* you have a real shared-blame sentence. If it’s flat, you say vendor, plus one line: *I pattern-matched the deploy. That was wrong.* That’s the clean version. Fake co-blame to protect your earlier sentence is the version that actually looks bad.
